clue.text: Got one's hands on roofing material?

definitions.meaning: touched or handled something, past tense of the verb meaning to sense by touch
the bitumen-soaked sheeting nailed onto sheds and flat roofs

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about grabbing hold of something used to cover a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: Past tense of the touch verb, and also the tarred fabric laid on shed roofs: two unrelated senses of one spelling.

clue.text: Saunter through street, reciting part

indicators.note: reciting is speaking out, so the word for a part is taken by its sound

parts.note: an actor's part is a role

explanation.surface: An actor wanders down the road running lines for a part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reciting' signals the word for a part is heard, not spelt: the homophone gives the bread-roll spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A saunter and a stroll are both unhurried, leisurely walks; the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Sporting a hat, before getting scarf

indicators.note: sporting in the playful, frolicking sense, so these letters romp into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone wears a hat first, then adds a scarf to the outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting' looks like 'wearing', but it signals rearranging A HAT BEFORE.
explanation.definitionFit: A long fluffy wrap of plumes worn round the neck is a kind of scarf: example of the category.

clue.text: See 27
Hob's drug-free, right? Fabulous!

parts.note: Hob is the setter, so the setter's means my

indicators.note: drug-free means without the drug, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: something morally right is ethical
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of being clean of drugs and asks for agreement, delighted.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often call themselves 'me' via their pseudonym. E is ecstasy, which 'free' removes.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabulous in its literal sense means belonging to fable or legend, the same as legendary or imaginary.

clue.text: Les Mis character backed ladies wearing denim?

definitions.note: the hero of Victor Hugo's novel Les Miserables

indicators.note: the reversed toilet is worn inside the double denim, so it sits within it

parts.note: a denim fabric; double denim, top and bottom, gives the fabric twice

indicators.note: backed means turned round, so the word for the toilet is written right to left

parts.note: the ladies is a women's toilet, a lav

explanation.surface: A question whether a stage character from the musical turned up in jeans, backing the women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' reverses the toilet word; 'wearing' sets it between two copies of the fabric, as in head-to-toe double denim. Liam Neeson played this part on film in 1998.
explanation.definitionFit: The ex-convict hero of Hugo's novel and the musical adapted from it is this named character.

clue.text: More tough and gutsy as MP once? That's right

parts.note: Ed Balls, a former Labour Member of Parliament
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a former politician was braver and tougher, and agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Balls was a UK Labour MP and minister until 2015.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballsy is slang for brave and spirited; this is its comparative form, matching the comparative phrase.

clue.text: Fellow has to go on runs

indicators.note: in a down entry, on means placed above, so the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: to go is a euphemism for to urinate
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A man must keep going to the toilet because of an upset stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runs' looks like diarrhoea in the surface, but it is just R, from cricket scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: A fellow is an equal or a member of the same group, which is the sense of a social equal.

clue.text: Green Man and Gawain are so alike — very jolly!

definitions.text: Green Man and Gawain are so alike
definitions.meaning: both names start with G and end with N, so they match only at their ends
British informal for very, as in jolly good

explanation.surface: Two figures of English legend, the Green Man and Sir Gawain, are said to be very similar: what fun!
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is cryptic: GREEN MAN and GAWAIN share only their outermost letters, G and N. 'Jolly' is British slang meaning very.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means to the utmost degree, interchangeable with the intensifiers very and jolly in British speech.

clue.text: Avoid reactionary English TV channel

indicators.note: reactionary suggests going backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: Dave is a British comedy and entertainment television channel

explanation.surface: Advice to steer clear of a conservative English television station.
explanation.walkthrough: Dave is a UK TV channel; 'reactionary' reverses E + DAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: To avoid something is to dodge or elude it; the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Swimmer's pace round bend

indicators.note: the pace goes round the bend, so its letters surround it

parts.note: a trot is a running pace, as of a horse
a U-bend is a sharp curve, so U stands for bend

explanation.surface: A swimmer's speed as they go round a turn in the course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' looks like a person, but it is a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A freshwater fish of the salmon family is a typical example of a creature that swims.

clue.text: One with a list of children's plays

indicators.note: plays means frolics or fools around, so these letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: Someone keeping a list of plays for children.
explanation.walkthrough: Oskar Schindler saved Jews by keeping them on his list of workers; Liam Neeson played him in Schindler's List.
explanation.definitionFit: The film title Schindler's List names the industrialist by the list he kept of workers he saved.

clue.text: See 6
Alive? No! Might have this internally

definitions.text: Alive? No! Might have this internally

indicators.note: internally says the answer lies inside the run of clue words

explanation.surface: Wondering if a victim survived: no, they may have poison inside them.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is inside aliVE NO Might, and the whole clue describes a fatal snake bite.
explanation.definitionFit: Poison injected by a bite or sting can leave someone not alive, so the clue defines the toxin by its deadly effect.

clue.text: Tom Hanks' son's carrying Latin dictionary

indicators.note: carrying means holding something within, so the abbreviation goes inside

parts.note: Colin Hanks, actor son of Tom Hanks, plus the possessive S

explanation.surface: An actor's son is carrying a Latin dictionary around.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Collins, Irish revolutionary, was played by Liam Neeson, and combines with 21-across.
explanation.definitionFit: A well-known British publisher of English-language reference books, so its name stands for a dictionary.

clue.text: House partly furious when briefed by new union member

indicators.note: briefed means cut short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: livid means furious
a bridegroom is one partner in a marriage union

explanation.surface: Part of a building was angry when told about a new trade union member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'union member' looks like a trade unionist, but the union is marriage. 'briefed' cuts LIVID to LIVI.
explanation.definitionFit: The lounge is one room of a house, so part of a home rather than the whole.

clue.text: Small top, say

parts.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
a peak is the top of a mountain

explanation.surface: A small top, for example, as in a garment size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' looks like 'for example' but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To say something is to utter it in words; the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Rich man born near Scottish resort to the west

indicators.note: in an across clue going west means right to left, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for born, as in genealogies
Oban is a seaside town and ferry port in western Scotland

explanation.surface: A wealthy man was born close to a Scottish holiday town on its western side.
explanation.walkthrough: Oban is a resort town on Scotland's west coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally an Indian governor, then a person of great wealth, especially one returned rich from India.

clue.text: Support placed over jaw, lip or cheek

indicators.note: in a down entry, placed over means written above the next piece

parts.note: to back someone is to support them
to jaw is to talk or chat

explanation.surface: A brace set over the jaw, lip or cheek, like a medical or dental device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jaw', 'lip' and 'cheek' read as parts of the face, but jaw is talk and lip and cheek are insolence.
explanation.definitionFit: Lip and cheek both mean impudent answering back, which is what insolent replies are.

clue.text: Playing Abraham Lincoln, heads for China

indicators.note: heads are the first letters, taken from each of the three words

explanation.surface: An actor playing Abraham Lincoln is off to China.
explanation.walkthrough: China means mate from Cockney rhyming slang, china plate. Liam Neeson was once cast to play Lincoln.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockney rhyming slang china plate means mate, so china is a friend or buddy.

clue.text: Cut up tough fish

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: to clip is to cut
hard means tough

explanation.surface: A command to chop a tough fish into pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut up' looks like chopping (or an anagram), but 'up' reverses CLIP to PILC.
explanation.definitionFit: A small oily sea fish related to the herring is one specific kind of fish.

clue.text: Boundary of river, generally

indicators.note: of signals the answer is made of letters from the following words

explanation.surface: The edge of a river, in general terms.
explanation.definitionFit: A verge is the edge or border of something, such as a grass strip beside a road.

clue.text: Name each limb cut off

indicators.note: off means wrong or awry, so the letters are rearranged
cut means the last letter is chopped from the word for a limb

explanation.surface: An instruction to name each limb that was amputated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' trims LIMB to LIM; 'off' then mixes EACH and LIM. Michael Collins was a Neeson title role.
explanation.definitionFit: A common boy's first name, so it is an example of a name.

clue.text: Report by male member, broadcast in Krung Thep

indicators.note: broadcast means spoken aloud, so the sound is what counts

parts.note: a report is a bang, followed by cock, slang for penis

explanation.surface: A news report by a male member of staff broadcast from the Thai capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'male member' looks like a man belonging to a group, but it is crude slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Krung Thep is what Thai speakers call their capital; foreigners know it by another name.

clue.text: Artist keeps recipe for soup

indicators.note: keeps means holds inside, so the abbreviation goes within the artist's name

parts.note: Hieronymus Bosch was a Dutch painter
R is the abbreviation for recipe, from Latin, on prescriptions

explanation.surface: A painter holds onto a soup recipe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eastern European beetroot dish is a well-known example of a soup.

clue.text: Relatives agreed about film

parts.note: kin are relatives

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: yes is said when agreeing

explanation.surface: Family members came to an agreement over a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning' but reverses YES to SEY. Liam Neeson starred as Alfred Kinsey in the 2004 film.
explanation.definitionFit: A 2004 biopic of sex researcher Alfred Kinsey bears his surname, so it is a film title.

clue.text: In general, a name for Scottish king?

parts.note: Mac begins many Scottish surnames, meaning son of
Arthur is the legendary king of Britain

explanation.surface: A query whether, in general, there is a Scottish name for a king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In general' looks like a phrase meaning usually, but general is the rank. Douglas MacArthur was a US general, played by Neeson in a 2016 Korean film.
explanation.definitionFit: Douglas MacArthur was an American five-star army commander, so his surname names a general.

clue.text: Sign a book

definitions.meaning: the second Gospel of the New Testament

explanation.surface: A request to put a signature in a book.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark is a sign or symbol, and the second Gospel is named after one of the evangelists.

clue.text: Waterside plant does climb?

indicators.note: in a down entry, to climb is to go up, so the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: does are female deer, so the plural stands for deer

explanation.surface: A puzzled question whether a riverside plant climbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'does' looks like a verb, but it is the plural of doe.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall grass that grows in marshes and beside water is a waterside plant.

clue.text: Back passage, right of the kidneys

indicators.note: Back means the word is written backwards

parts.note: a lane is a narrow passage or way

explanation.surface: A back alley on the right, oddly linked to kidney anatomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back passage' tempts as one phrase, but 'Back' reverses LANE.
explanation.definitionFit: The medical adjective describes things relating to the kidneys, from Latin renes.

clue.text: One male's in different roles of his here

definitions.text: One male's in different roles of his here

indicators.note: different means changed, so these letters take a new order

explanation.surface: An actor appears in several of his own film roles in this grid.
explanation.walkthrough: The grid is full of the Northern Irish actor's roles: Schindler, Collins, Kinsey, Valjean, Rob Roy, MacArthur.
explanation.definitionFit: Northern Irish film star who played Schindler, Michael Collins and Valjean, roles placed throughout the grid.

clue.text: Formerly Rob Roy's lead part? Not originally

indicators.note: the lead of a word is its opening letter
not originally means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: to part is to leave or depart

explanation.surface: A question whether Rob Roy was the leading role, though not at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rob Roy' reads as one name, the Scottish outlaw Neeson played, but splits: 'Formerly Rob' is the definition, and 'Not originally' drops the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic verb meaning to plunder or carry off by force, so an old word for robbing.

clue.text: Sweet sticky stuff works for Tommy?

parts.note: rock is the hard sugary stick sold at British seaside resorts
opera is the plural of opus, a work

explanation.surface: A sticky sweet is suitable for a boy called Tommy.
explanation.walkthrough: British seaside rock is a hard candy stick. The Who's Tommy is the classic example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Who's 1969 album telling a story through songs is a famous example of the genre.
